name: Address Field Decomposition (Tag / Set-Index / Offset)
recognitionClueHinglish: Agar question me diya hai: cache size, block size, associativity (direct-mapped / k-way / fully-associative), aur total address width (ya main memory size) — aur poocha hai TAG/SET/INDEX/WORD/OFFSET field me kitne bits hain — to ye is pattern ka sabse classic question hai. Yehi single sabse-zyada-repeat-hone-wala GATE cache pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Step 2: #lines = cache size / block size; #sets = #lines / associativity
Step 3: Set/index bits = log2(#sets) (0 if fully associative, since there's only 1 'set')
Step 4: Tag bits = total address bits − offset bits − index bits
Sanity check: tag + index + offset MUST equal total address width.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Note down: total address bits (A), cache size (C), block size (B), associativity (k) — convert everything to consistent units (bytes or words) first, this is where most silly mistakes happen.
2. offset = log2(B)
3. number of lines = C / B
4. number of sets = (number of lines) / k   [k=1 for direct-mapped, k=∞/1-set for fully-associative]
5. index/set bits = log2(number of sets)
6. tag bits = A − offset − index
7. Double-check with the identity tag+index+offset = A.
variationsObserved: Given main memory size instead of address width directly (need log2(memory size) first).
Byte-addressable vs word-addressable memory — changes what the 'offset' actually measures.
Question gives TAG bits and asks you to back-solve for associativity or cache size (reverse direction of the same formula).
2D array traversal wrapped around this (see pattern 04) where the array's memory layout feeds into the address split.
commonTraps: Not converting KB/MB consistently (1K = 2^10, not 1000, in this context).
Treating 'number of lines' as 'number of sets' directly for a set-associative cache.
Forgetting the extra bits needed for byte-offset within a word when block size is given in words but memory is byte-addressable.
edgeCases: Fully-associative: index bits = 0 always, tag = A − offset.

name: AMAT / Multi-Level Cache Hierarchy Access Time
recognitionClueHinglish: Agar question me L1/L2 (ya cache + main memory) ke hit rates aur access times diye hain aur 'average access time' ya 'effective access time' poocha hai — ye AMAT pattern hai. Do-level se teen-level tak ho sakta hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: AMAT = Hit time + Miss rate × Miss penalty
Miss penalty at level i = AMAT of level (i+1) — recursion chalti hai neeche tak
Draw the hit/miss tree before plugging into the formula.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify the number of levels (L1, L2, ..., main memory).
2. Start from the LAST level (main memory access time is just its own access time — no 'miss' beyond it).
3. Compute AMAT of the second-to-last level using: hit_time + miss_rate × (AMAT of next level).
4. Work backward level by level until you reach L1's AMAT — that's the final answer.
5. If the question instead gives 'local miss rate' vs 'global miss rate', clarify which one is used in the formula — local miss rate is what plugs directly into this recursive formula.
variationsObserved: Asked as 'effective CPI impact' instead of raw time (multiply the miss-penalty-in-time term by clock frequency to convert to cycles, then fold into CPI).
Given bandwidth + latency instead of a flat access time (compute time = latency + size/bandwidth first).
Speedup-style framing: 'by what factor does adding this cache improve performance' — same AMAT machinery, just take the ratio of before/after.
commonTraps: Using GLOBAL miss rate at an inner level when the formula needs LOCAL miss rate (or vice versa) — always check which one the question defines.
Forgetting to add hit_time even when miss_rate is being processed — hit time is paid on EVERY access, hit or miss.
Unit mismatch: mixing ns and clock cycles without converting via clock frequency.
edgeCases: Single-level cache is just AMAT = hit_time + miss_rate × miss_penalty with miss_penalty given directly (no further recursion).

name: Replacement-Policy Trace (LRU/FIFO block-reference simulation)
recognitionClueHinglish: Agar question me memory-block references ki ek sequence di hai (jaise '0,1,2,3,0,4,...') aur poocha hai ki kaunsa block cache me RAHEGA ya kitne MISSES honge, given a replacement policy (mostly LRU) — ye simulation/trace pattern hai. Isme formula nahi, step-by-step haath se trace karna padta hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Draw a table: one row per reference, columns = cache lines/sets.
On every reference: is the block already present? HIT (update recency) else MISS (evict per policy, insert new block).
For set-associative, only worry about the ONE set that block maps to — reduce the problem to a smaller direct/fully-associative trace within that set.
conceptsRequired: Set-associative mapping (which set a block belongs to)
generalSolvingApproach: 1. If set-associative, first compute which SET each referenced block maps to (block number mod number-of-sets).
2. Group the reference sequence by set — only references to the SAME set interact with each other.

3. Within one set, simulate LRU: maintain an ordered list (most-recent to least-recent); on hit, move block to front; on miss with full set, evict the back (least-recent) and insert new block at front.
4. Count misses / read off final cache contents as asked.
variationsObserved: FIFO instead of LRU (evict oldest-INSERTED, not oldest-USED — different from LRU when there are repeated hits).
Question asks 'which block will NOT be in the cache' instead of the miss count — same trace, different final read-off.
commonTraps: Mixing FIFO and LRU behavior — FIFO ignores hits for eviction order, LRU doesn't.
Forgetting that different sets are INDEPENDENT — a reference to set 2 does not affect set 0's LRU order.
edgeCases: Fully-associative cache = the whole cache is one set, so the trace applies to all blocks directly.

name: Loop/Array Traversal Cache-Performance Analysis (row-major vs column-major, code-segment comparison)
recognitionClueHinglish: Agar question me C code diya hai jisme nested for-loop se 2D array traverse ho raha hai (do versions P1 aur P2, jaise i-then-j vs j-then-i order), aur poocha hai kaunsa version zyada cache-friendly hai ya kitne hits/misses honge — ye locality-of-reference application hai, address-split pattern ke sath combine hota hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: C arrays are stored ROW-MAJOR — traversing row-by-row (i outer, j inner) accesses consecutive memory addresses → good spatial locality.
Traversing column-by-column (j outer, i inner) jumps by (row-size) addresses each step → poor spatial locality → more misses.
Combine with Pattern 01: figure out how many array elements fit in one cache block, that tells you how many consecutive accesses are 'free' (hits) before the next miss.
conceptsRequired: Pattern 01 (address split, to know block size in elements)
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Determine array storage order (row-major, given as default for C unless stated otherwise) and element size.
2. Compute how many array elements fit per cache block = block size / element size.
3. For the GOOD traversal order (matches storage order): every (elements-per-block)-th access is a miss, rest are hits.
4. For the BAD traversal order (against storage order): almost every access is a miss (each element lands in a different block).
variationsObserved: Two-loop comparison (P1 vs P2) asking which has fewer misses, vs a single-loop version asking for the exact miss count.
Combined with direct-mapped index-conflict: even the 'good' row-major order can thrash if the row length causes different rows to map to the SAME cache line.
commonTraps: Assuming row-major traversal is ALWAYS all-hits-after-first — if the array is large enough that consecutive rows alias to the same cache set/line, you get conflict misses even in the 'good' order.
Forgetting array indexing starts at 0 when computing addresses.
edgeCases: Array size much larger than cache — every new row may evict the previous one before reuse, changing the analysis.

name: Write Policy / Inclusion Property / Coherence — Conceptual (True-False / MSQ style)
recognitionClueHinglish: Agar question me numerical calculation nahi hai, balki statements diye hain about write-through/write-back, dirty bit, inclusion property, ya cache coherence, aur poocha hai kaunse statements TRUE hain — ye conceptual/MSQ pattern hai, GATE 2020 ke baad ye zyada common ho gaya hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Write-through: every write goes to memory immediately → simpler, more bus traffic, no dirty bit needed.
Write-back: write stays in cache, dirty bit set, flushed to memory only on eviction → less bus traffic, needs dirty bit + write-back on evict.
Inclusion property: L2 ⊇ L1 (everything in L1 also in L2) is needed for cache-coherence protocols to only need to snoop L2.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. For each statement, mentally classify it under one of: write-policy behavior, replacement-policy behavior, or inclusion/coherence behavior.
2. Check it against the definitions above — most traps are simple reversals (swapping write-through and write-back behavior).
3. For MSQ, evaluate each option independently — don't assume the count of correct options.
variationsObserved: Combined with TLB/MMU (virtual vs physical addressed cache) — cross-links to Virtual Memory topic.
commonTraps: Assuming inclusion is automatic — it must be actively maintained by the replacement policy.

name: Basic Definition / Principle of Locality (rare now, mostly pre-2000 descriptive)
recognitionClueHinglish: 'What is cache memory', 'principle of locality justifies use of ___' jaise seedhe definitional questions — GATE ke bahut purane papers (1987-1995) me the, ab MCQ/NAT era me lagbhag nahi aate directly, lekin concept clarity ke liye zaroori hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Cache = small fast memory exploiting locality of reference to reduce AMAT.
generalSolvingApproach: Direct recall — no calculation needed.
